extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and their representatives (attorneys/agents) and USPTO petition filers/examiners handling revival petitions under 37 CFR 1.137
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for filing and evaluating petitions to revive U.S. patent applications abandoned under 37 CFR 1.137 (unavoidable or unintentional delay), including required contents, timelines, burdens of proof, and evidence standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and standard for 'unavoidable' delay
rubrics_metrics.description: “Unavoidable” delay is the epitome of “unintentional” delay. Decisions on reviving abandoned applications on the basis of “unavoidable” delay have adopted the reasonably prudent person standard: reliance upon the ordinary and trustworthy agencies of mail and telegraph, worthy and reliable employees, and such other means and instrumentalities as are usually employed in such important business; if unexpectedly or through unforeseen fault these agencies fail, the failure may be unavoidable if all other conditions of promptness in rectification are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An intentional delay precludes revival under 37 CFR 1.137(a) or (b). Decisions are made case-by-case taking all facts and circumstances into account; the petitioner bears the burden of establishing the delay was unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical/employee error may support 'unavoidable' delay if conditions met
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from an error (e.g., a docketing error) on the part of an employee in the performance of a clerical function may provide the basis for a showing of 'unavoidable' delay, provided it is shown that: (A) the error was the cause of the delay at issue; (B) there was in place a business routine for performing the clerical function that could reasonably be relied upon to avoid errors in its performance; and (C) the employee was sufficiently trained and experienced with regard to the function and routine for its performance that reliance upon such employee represented the exercise of due care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Egbers, In re Katrapat, and related decisions for examples. The petitioner must make factual showings on each element to support unavoidable delay based on clerical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper notification of change of correspondence address
rubrics_metrics.description: To show unavoidable delay where abandonment resulted from change of correspondence address, an adequate showing must include that due care was taken to adhere to the requirement for prompt notification in each concerned application and must include an adequate showing that a timely notification of the change of address was filed in the application concerned in a manner reasonably calculated to call attention to the fact that it was a notification of a change of address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The following do NOT constitute proper notification: (A) mere inclusion, in a paper filed for another purpose, of an address differing from the previously provided correspondence address without mention that an address change was being made; (B) notification on a paper listing plural applications as affected (except Customer Number practice); (C) lack of notification, or belated notification, to the USPTO of the change in correspondence address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delays caused by lack of legal knowledge or improper application of rules do not constitute 'unavoidable' delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay resulting from the lack of knowledge or improper application of the patent statute, rules of practice or the MPEP does not constitute 'unavoidable' delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: permitting the maximum extendable period while awaiting allowance, failing to file papers/fees per 37 CFR 1.8/1.10, reliance on oral advice from USPTO employees, or USPTO failure to advise in time — none render delay unavoidable. Cite Haines, Vincent v. Mossinghoff, Smith v. Diamond, Potter v. Dann, In re Sivertz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three delay periods to evaluate under 37 CFR 1.137
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three periods to consider in evaluating a petition under 37 CFR 1.137: (A) the delay in reply that originally resulted in the abandonment; (B) the delay in filing an initial petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137 to revive the application; and (C) the delay in filing a grantable petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137 to revive the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner must address the entire timeline from the original missed reply through the filing of a grantable petition; unavoidable/unintentional must be shown for the entire delay period as required by statutes and 37 CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness in filing petition and timing safe-harbors (3 months / 1 year)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office generally will not question whether there has been intentional delay when a petition under 37 CFR 1.137 is filed (A) within 3 months of the date the applicant is first notified that the application is abandoned; and (B) within 1 year of the date of abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are advised to file within 3 months of first notification to avoid issues of intentional delay. If a petition is not filed within 3 months, the Office may require showings regarding how the delay between notification and petition filing was 'unavoidable' (for (a)) or 'unintentional' (for (b)). If not filed within 1 year, the Office will require further information about when the applicant first became aware and show how discovery of abandonment occurred despite due care/diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate abandonment or deliberate delay precludes relief
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandonment of an application considered to be a deliberately chosen course of action, or deliberate choice not to seek or persist in seeking revival (or deliberate delay in seeking revival), precludes a finding of unavoidable or unintentional delay pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional decisions (e.g., delaying revival until industry/competitor interest arises) are fatal to petitions regardless of correctness of prior Office actions or new information discovered after abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: The relevant party whose delay is considered
rubrics_metrics.description: The question under 37 CFR 1.137 is whether the delay on the part of the party having the right or authority to reply to avoid abandonment (or not reply) was unavoidable or unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant assigned all rights to a third party, the applicant’s delay is irrelevant. If a third party controls prosecution (assignee, licensee, etc.), the third party’s decision is binding on the applicant unless the contract expressly limits the third party to fiduciary-only conduct; otherwise the applicant is bound by the actions/inactions of the third party. Cite Kim v. Quigg, Winkler, Futures Technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(a) and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137(a)(3) requires a showing to the satisfaction of the Director that the entire delay from the due date for the reply until the filing of a grantable petition was unavoidable. 37 CFR 1.137(b)(3) requires a statement that the entire delay was unintentional; the Director may require additional information where there is a question whether the delay was unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the petitioner must carry the burden of proof in (a) petitions. For (b) petitions the Office will generally accept the required statement but may require the applicant to produce additional evidence and carry the burden if there is doubt about whether the entire delay was unintentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents for a grantable petition (Form PTO/SB/61)
rubrics_metrics.description: A grantable petition requires the following items: (1) Petition fee; (2) Reply and/or issue fee; (3) Terminal disclaimer with disclaimer fee – required for all utility and plant applications filed before June 8, 1995, and for all design applications; and (4) Adequate showing of the cause of unavoidable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form PTO/SB/61 (and PTO/SB/61PCT) may be used. The form contains certificate of mailing/transmission options and requires signatures and, when applicable, additional sheets containing statements establishing unavoidable delay. Warning: avoid submitting personal information (SSNs, bank account numbers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirement for 37 CFR 1.137 petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137(d) requires that a petition under either 37 CFR 1.137(a) or 1.137(b) be accompanied by a terminal disclaimer (and fee), regardless of the period of abandonment, in specified circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners must comply with the terminal disclaimer rules and pay any applicable disclaimer fee. (The MPEP provides further specifics on when a terminal disclaimer is required.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Showings required when petition is not timely filed (additional factual detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(a) or (b) is not filed within 3 months of notification or not filed within 1 year of abandonment, the Office will require additional showings: e.g., how the delay between notification and petition filing was 'unavoidable' or how the delay in discovering the abandoned status occurred despite due care or diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should include the date they first became aware of the abandonment and a detailed showing of how discovery of the abandonment occurred despite exercise of due care; failure to meet the burden to establish the entire delay was unavoidable/unintentional may lead to denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy/confidentiality and avoidance of personal identifying information
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal information such as social security numbers, bank account numbers, or credit card numbers (other than a check or credit card authorization form PTO-2038 submitted for payment purposes) is never required by the USPTO to support a petition or an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners/applicants are cautioned to avoid submitting personal information that may contribute to identity theft and should consider redacting such information. Records become public after publication or issuance and abandoned application records may be public if referenced; checks and PTO-2038 forms are not retained in the application file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of mailing/transmission options for filing petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition form includes a CERTIFICATE OF MAILING OR TRANSMISSION (37 CFR 1.8(a)) whereby correspondence may be: deposited with the United States Postal Service as first-class mail addressed to Mail Stop Petition, Commissioner for Patents, P.O. Box 1450, Alexandria, VA 22313-1450; or transmitted by facsimile to the USPTO at the specified fax number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the date and signature on the certificate. The form also provides telephone/facsimile contact information for assistance completing the form.
